overall_summary: Deduplicated analysis of the FACTVERSE channel performance clearly indicates that high-concept astronomy, extreme planetary extremes, and hypothetical 'What If' space scenarios are heavily outperforming standard Earth biology or psychological tricks. Specifically, recent videos touching on bizarre cosmic phenomena (e.g., Venus day lengths, liquid diamond planets, and extreme dark planets) command the highest views and engagement velocity within the critical 7-day performance window.

winning_patterns.pattern: Hypothetical Cosmic 'What If' & Extreme Planet Scenarios
winning_patterns.evidence: Videos like 'What If You Fell Into a Liquid Diamond Planet?' (1,029 views, 38 likes) and 'Venus Has a Day Longer Than Its Year' (981 views, 21 likes) show exceptionally high view counts and engagement ratios compared to standard earth facts.
winning_patterns.action: Double down on surreal astronomical scenarios that challenge human intuition, framing them as immersive thought experiments.

winning_patterns.evidence: Titles featuring unusual matter behaviors like 'The Planet of Burning Ice' (972 views) or 'This Planet Rains Supersonic Rubies!' (723 views) capture high click-through and sustained viewer interest.
winning_patterns.action: Continue pairing exotic materials (rubies, glass, diamond, burning ice) with extreme planetary weather conditions.

weak_patterns.evidence: Shorts like 'Your Brain Can Create Fake Memories' (5 views) and 'The Real Reason Songs Get Stuck In Your Head' (17 views) generated negligible engagement relative to space content.
weak_patterns.action: De-prioritize psychological micro-facts unless they involve deeply unsettling or counter-intuitive paradoxes.

weak_patterns.evidence: Basic animal facts like 'Octopuses Have THREE Hearts' published earlier gained modest traction, but newer iterations show declining velocity compared to space scaling.
weak_patterns.action: Pivot animal survival concepts toward cinematic, high-stakes environmental survival rather than static anatomical trivia.
